text: From DFT to atomic forces: finite differences, independent references, force convergence and the BOMD interface Atomic forces are obtained as position derivatives of the total energy in a multiatom periodic He cell. Analytic gradients, finite differences of energies and an independent plane-wave calculation are compared, separating orbital-basis, k-point, auxiliary-grid and SCF effects on forces. The requirements for a BOMD force interface are distinguished from the additional validation of trajectories. This educational verification uses a fixed cell, a local He GTH potential and spin-unpolarized LDA. It is an execution and validation driver using PySCF analytic nuclear gradients, rather than a new electronic-structure engine. Agreement for this configuration does not validate other elements, nonlocal pseudopotentials, stress, long BOMD trajectories or thermostats. On this page Stored measurements: finite differences, independent references and force convergence These stored results come from the release’s fixed input. Force comparisons use the maximum absolute difference over Cartesian components in hartree/bohr unless stated otherwise. Sweeps reuse common settings; setting counts are not distinct physical problems. Acceptance uses unrounded values. Wide numeric tables scroll horizontally within their own region. Full results / JSON · Settings and forces / CSV · Independent reference and convergence / JSON Forces are negative gradients of the total energy For a fixed lattice, electron count, functional and pseudopotential, the electronic ground state is solved at each atomic configuration. The Born–Oppenheimer energy is the total cell energy, including electronic and periodic ion–ion terms. The force on Cartesian component α of atom I is minus the total derivative with respect to that coordinate. Gradient and force signs must be distinguished: coordinates in bohr and energies in hartree give forces in hartree/bohr. The input is a cubic cell of side 5 bohr with He positions (0.37, 0.61, 0.83) and (2.13, 2.27, 2.41) bohr: four valence electrons in a closed-shell fixed configuration. It avoids a check in which symmetry makes every force zero. Directions and all x, y and z components are compared, as well as magnitudes. Numerical agreement for this artificial arrangement does not predict an equilibrium helium crystal or establish chemical accuracy. Stress and pressure require cell derivatives, separate from atomic-position derivatives at fixed cell. Feynman (1939) The Hellmann–Feynman theorem and Pulay terms from moving bases For a normalized exact eigenstate, the energy derivative with respect to a parameter equals the expectation of the Hamiltonian derivative. This is the Hellmann–Feynman relation. Feynman’s 1939 paper is a historical primary source for evaluating molecular forces directly. The theorem alone does not make every force correct for an electronic state represented in a finite atom-centered basis. The H and Ψ below express the general theorem; they do not replace the Kohn–Sham total energy by a sum of orbital eigenvalues. A Gaussian basis moving with the atoms changes its functions and overlap matrix when nuclei move. Even with variationally optimized orbital coefficients, derivatives of this basis dependence must be included when differentiating the discrete energy. These are Pulay terms. The overlap derivative contracted with an energy-weighted density in the generalized eigenproblem is one contribution. The driver uses PySCF analytic nuclear gradients; it does not substitute a bare electron–ion Coulomb force. At fixed cell and cutoff, plane waves do not move with atomic positions. Finite-cutoff force errors nevertheless remain, and SCF and density-grid errors must still be controlled. The absence of moving-atom basis terms does not make plane-wave forces exact. Basis changes under cell deformation and Pulay stress are distinct from this fixed-cell test. Pulay (1969), PySCF developers (2026), DFTK developers (2026) Finite-difference checks: smaller displacements are not always better One Cartesian component of one atom is displaced by ±h from the baseline configuration. At each displaced geometry the SCF is converged independently, and the resulting total energies give a central-difference force. The lattice, k points and weights, basis name, FFT grid, functional, pseudopotential and electron count are aligned. The atom-centered basis moves too, so this probes derivatives of the same discrete energy including basis-position dependence. For a smooth energy surface, central-difference truncation is O(h²). SCF solution and roundoff errors in energies are divided by 2h, so very small displacements can increase errors. Several h values are retained to locate a stable agreement range with analytic forces. A clean U-shaped measured curve is not assumed. An input SCF energy tolerance is not interpreted as a rigorous bound on the error of each energy. Agreement with finite differences from the same engine checks internal consistency, including signs, components and basis derivatives. Both use shared functional and pseudopotential implementations, so this alone is not an independent physical reference. A separate plane-wave DFTK implementation provides the independent comparison here. Pulay (1969), PySCF developers (2026) Converge basis, k points, auxiliary grids and SCF for forces separately A small energy change alone does not establish converged forces. The Gaussian orbital basis, Brillouin-zone mesh, auxiliary FFT grid and SCF stopping conditions are varied one at a time, comparing forces on the same atoms and Cartesian components. Atom ordering and axes are fixed. Summaries use an L∞-type maximum absolute component norm, distinct from a per-atom vector magnitude or a component average. Increasing a basis’s zeta label does not necessarily produce nested spaces or monotonic force changes. Nor are all k meshes nested. The final pair of settings is compared with a published target, without presenting the increment as a rigorous complete-basis or infinite-k-point error bound. The auxiliary FFT representation of density and local potentials is a separate convergence axis from the Gaussian orbital space. Incomplete SCF convergence also affects forces. Alongside termination flags and iteration counts, inspect stored electron-count, orbital and SCF residual diagnostics. Force sensitivity to tighter stopping conditions is measured directly, and an unconverged electronic state must not be returned to BOMD as an accepted force. Each sweep varies one control while holding the other controls at the finite settings specified in the public input. Basis sequences are checked separately at Γ and 2³, but no joint calculation combines 4³ sampling, the largest Gaussian basis and the finest FFT grid. Head-Gordon (2005) Independent reference: the same model in a different discretization PySCF uses a periodic Gaussian basis and FFTDF; the reference uses DFTK’s plane-wave Hamiltonian, SCF, periodic ion interactions and analytic forces. Lattice and all atomic positions, valence count, spin restriction and integer occupations, every local-GTH coefficient, Libxc LDA_X plus LDA_C_VWN (VWN5), fractional k points and weights are matched. No fitted energy offset or force correction is applied. The DFTK plane-wave cutoff is increased separately and its final force increment is measured. This is not a rounding-error comparison of identical finite matrices. Different finite Gaussian and plane-wave spaces are assessed using the published acceptance width and convergence diagnostics on both sides. Both engines share Libxc, which limits the extent of implementation independence. DFTK compute_forces returns a representation associated with fractional coordinates; the Cartesian API is compute_forces_cart. Coordinate and force transformations are different. Comparisons here use Cartesian components in hartree/bohr throughout. The generation script, pinned Julia environment, pseudopotential, input and result hashes are retained. Cancès (2021), DFTK developers (2026) Check components, translation and nonzero forces A configuration with nearly zero forces can pass even with a sign error. A multiatom configuration carrying nonzero forces is used, with componentwise comparisons of analytic forces, finite differences and the independent reference. A single force norm should not hide component permutations, atom-order mistakes or incorrect units. In an ideal periodic system without external fields, uniform translation leaves the total energy unchanged and the sum of atomic forces vanishes. Finite real-space grids can numerically break this property; the remaining total force is a useful grid and differentiation diagnostic. Translation checks alone do not establish accurate relative forces, so energy differences and an independent reference are used alongside them. E({RI+t})=E({RI})⟹∑IFI=0E({RI​+t})=E({RI​})⟹I∑​FI​=0 Sources: DFTK developers (2026), PySCF developers (2026) The BOMD interface and additional trajectory validation The BOMD force provider energy_and_forces accepts positions_bohr and returns energy_per_cell and forces_cartesian from the same energy surface, together with SCF convergence and residual diagnostics. An unconverged electronic state is treated as a failure. Masses belong to nuclear time integration, not as factors multiplying the DFT potential energy or forces. Wrapped positions inside a periodic cell must be distinguished from a continuous trajectory record. Velocity Verlet advances velocities by half a step, updates positions, solves the electronic problem again for the new forces, then completes the velocity update. Carrying an electronic guess from a previous step accelerates the calculation but does not replace SCF convergence. This verification focuses on atomic forces and the BOMD handoff; a single force evaluation or short interface smoke test is not counted as validation of long trajectories. Accepting a practical trajectory additionally requires timestep refinement, tighter-SCF comparisons, total-energy and momentum checks in unthermostatted NVE, and time-reversal checks where appropriate. Thermostats can hide force or integration errors by absorbing energy changes, so unthermostatted checks come first. Small short-time drift does not guarantee long-time stability or a correct statistical distribution. Car–Parrinello dynamics is a distinct formulation propagating fictitious electronic degrees of freedom alongside nuclei. A force provider on the Born–Oppenheimer surface is not a CPMD implementation. The cross-field navigation separately shows the executed scope of DFT, force evaluation, nuclear integration and temperature control. The method registry also links a separate two-state BO/CP-type educational model.
